title: US and China Extend Trade Truce Two Months as Xi Lands in Washington, While the Senate Tries to Force a Vote on China-Chip Bills
subhead: Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the US and China agreed to extend their trade truce for two more months as Xi Jinping begins his Washington state visit, while lawmakers press for a Senate vote on legislation to tighten China's access to AI chips.

sections.heading: Trade Truce Extended as Xi Arrives in Washington
sections.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing have agreed to extend their trade truce by two months, to January 10, and pledged to work toward a bigger deal, just as Chinese President Xi Jinping began his state visit to Washington. Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC and Nikkei Asia all reported the extension on Wednesday evening, with Bloomberg citing the January 10 date directly.

Markets opened mixed on Thursday as Xi arrived for the talks, France 24 reported, reflecting the uncertainty around whether this round produces substance or simply buys more time. The two-month extension follows a weekend of escalation-announcements and de-escalation signals, and it frames Xi's visit as the pivotal moment for whether the ceasefire hardens into a structured arrangement on tariffs, technology and critical minerals.
sections.whyItMatters: The truce buys breathing room but sets up January as a hard deadline. With chip export policy, rare earths and AI access all unresolved, the extension keeps the summit's stakes high without resolving any of the underlying fights.

sections.heading: Senate Democrats Push to Force a Vote on China-Chip Bills
sections.body:
On Capitol Hill, a legislative push to tighten China's access to advanced chips moved to the foreground. Politico reported Wednesday that Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer is pressing Majority Leader-elect John Thune for a floor vote on chip export bills, while the Washington Times reported Senate Democrats are pushing a trio of bills to block China from AI chips. A separate report flagged that the bipartisan measures could face delay in reaching the Senate floor, per Seeking Alpha and TradingView.

The Hill, citing senior Senate Democrats, reported Tuesday that the administration is failing to block China's access to American AI technology — a claim that gives this legislative effort momentum heading into the summit. The legislation would sit alongside executive-branch export controls as a statutory backstop, but its fate rests on floor timing that remains uncertain.
sections.whyItMatters: The fight over China-chip policy is shifting from White House rules to Congress. A Senate vote would lock in restrictions that a single administration could otherwise loosen, but the reported delay shows how summit diplomacy and legislative momentum are colliding.

sections.heading: AI Safety Talks on the Table, but Neither Side Wants to Slow Down
sections.body:
AI is central to the summit agenda, but the two sides are approaching it from very different assumptions. CNBC reported Wednesday that the Trump-Xi meeting puts AI safety talks on the table while neither side wants to slow its own development. The Guardian described AI as looming large over the meeting amid deep distrust between Washington and Beijing.

The concrete proposal on the table is a US offer to establish an AI safety notification mechanism — an early-warning channel for model incidents or deployments — floated by Bessent in talks since Monday, according to Al Jazeera, NBC News and CNN. The mechanism would amount to a communications link rather than an arms-control ceiling: both governments see advantage in avoiding catastrophic surprises, but neither is willing to constrain its own compute buildup or export posture to get there.
sections.whyItMatters: AI safety is becoming a rare area of possible US-China cooperation, separate from the competition over compute and chips. A notification channel would be a modest but real first step toward managing a race both sides insist they will win rather than slow.

sections.heading: Rare Earths and Critical Minerals Loom Over the Talks
sections.body:
China's control of rare earth processing is shaping up as one of the summit's flashpoints. The New York Times reported Tuesday that China's continued grip on rare earths is looming over the Trump-Xi meeting, and a US News feature framed the talks as unfolding 'under the shadow of AI, trade and rare earth tensions'.

The stakes sharpen with Beijing's looming November export controls, which S&P Global and Fastmarkets have flagged as a test of rare-earth refining and recycling capacity outside China. Analysts at CFR have been framing the issue as a supply-chain weapon that Washington struggles to defuse, while The Conversation noted how the US ceded processing leadership over decades. A Maryland Daily Record report Wednesday described critical minerals as a hinge issue for the summit outcome.
sections.whyItMatters: Rare earths are the leverage Beijing holds that chips cannot cover. November's controls arrive just as the trade truce's January deadline approaches, meaning the summit's outcomes on minerals will shape whether the truce even survives its own calendar.

sections.heading: On the Compute Side: Huawei Scales Up Even as It Curbs AI Exports
sections.body:
Beyond the summit politics, China's own AI-compute buildout keeps advancing. A niche industry report Wednesday claimed Huawei's Atlas cluster has reached 120 exaflops of aggregated AI compute while the company curbs exports of its AI systems — a figure that needs independent confirmation. The stronger, better-sourced datapoint came from South China Morning Post, citing a Bernstein analysis that Huawei's mobile chip is narrowing the gap with Apple through its Tau Scaling Law architecture.

The pattern across these reports is consistent with what Alibaba's Zhenwu V900 and DeepSeek's shift to domestic chips already signaled: China is building export-restricted but rapidly maturing domestic silicon, and now beginning to manage its own AI-hardware exports as supplies tighten domestically.
sections.whyItMatters: Huawei moving from pure import-substitution to managing its own AI exports marks a threshold: Chinese compute is no longer just a response to US controls but an independent supply pool with its own allocation choices.

bottomLine: Today's real development is political: Washington and Beijing extended the trade truce by two months as Xi arrived in Washington, the Senate moved to force votes on China-chip legislation, and both sides tabled an AI-safety notification channel even as neither will slow its own buildup. The summit frame is now set — AI safety as a possible channel, rare earths and chips as the unresolved substance, and a January deadline behind it all. The two months bought by the truce will be spent not on de-escalation but on defining what each side is actually willing to trade.
